newsitem.title: FRANCE: French parties trade blame for National Front win.
newsitem.headline: French parties trade blame for National Front win.

text.p: France's mainstream parties, looking anxiously to a general election in 13 months' time, traded blame on Monday over who let the extreme-right National Front win control of a fourth southern town.

The stunning victory of Catherine Megret, 37, wife of the anti-immigration party's number two, in a municipal election in Vitrolles, a soulless commuter town north of Marseille, was a shock, if not a surprise, to the French political establishment.

Despite calls for a national mobilisation against the Front, Megret, whose husband Bruno made no secret that he would wield the real power, beat sleaze-tainted Socialist Jean-Jacques Anglade by 52.48 percent to 47.52 in Sunday's runoff vote.
Centre-right cabinet ministers played down the result as a local phenomenon due to a discredited Socialist incumbent.

"Without diminishing an election result, it must be kept in proportion...We are looking at a very particular situation where the National Front has exploited a difficult situation," centrist Labour and Social Affairs Minister Jacques Barrot said.

Socialist Party number two Daniel Vaillant acknowledged that Anglade was a problem but attributed Megret's win to the failure of mainstream conservatives to back the "anti-fascist" candidate in sufficient numbers.

Political scientists said it was the first time the National Front had won a head-to-head runoff with an absolute majority. Its previous successes had been in triangular contests against mainstream left and right-wing candidates.

Coming on top of 1995 victories in the nearby towns of Toulon, Orange and Marignane, it showed how deeply the party of Jean-Marie Le Pen has taken root in the southeast Provence-Alpes-Cote d'Azur region with its explosive mix of crime, corruption, Arab immigration and a high density of former French settlers from North Africa.
"Who can say that the National Front is not capable of becoming France's first party? If you judge from the Vitrolles microcosm, you realise that it's possible," Le Pen exulted.
But analysts said the movement, which advocates expelling three million immigrants and reserving jobs, housing and welfare benefits for French nationals, was far from that goal.

"The Vitrolles municipal election result justifies neither the National Front's boasting nor the wailing of the defeated so-called republicans," editorialist Georges Suffert wrote in the conservative daily Le Figaro.

Pollsters said national support for the Front had barely increased since Le Pen won 15 percent in the 1995 presidential election. The party lost several recent elections against better mainstream candidates.
Nevertheless, they said, the Front could win enough votes to influence the outcome of the March 1998 general election by maintaining its candidates on the second round in up to 200 constituencies.
Socialist leaders pointed to local factors in Vitrolles, a high-rise new town with 22 percent unemployment, a high crime rate and a poorly integrated immigrant community.

But analyst Jean-Marc Lerch of the IPSOS polling institute said the Front was now winning votes more because of its charges of corruption against the political establishment than due to its traditional themes of immigration and insecurity.
Opinion polls showed that voters gave the government high marks for combating illegal immigration and delinquency, but all the major parties were increasingly viewed as corrupt.

Le Pen stepped up his attacks in a radio interview on Sunday night, denouncing what he called "the high levels of corruption of French political circles and especially of the party presided over by Mr Chirac and perhaps of Chirac himself".

He referred to the numerous judicial investigations into allegations that the Gaullist RPR party was funded by kickbacks on housing and public works contracts while Chirac was mayor of Paris from 1977 to 1995.
